claim: Nine patients with refractory epilepsy participated in 40 sessions of an associative episodic memory task.
source: Nine patients with refractory epilepsy volunteered to participate in the experiments. Mean age of patients was 37 years (s.d.: 9.1; range: 26–53). All but two patients were right-handed. On average, patients suffered 15.6 years from epilepsy. All patients had temporal lobe epilepsy with either a left (N=3), right (N=3)m or bilateral focus (N=3). Each patient participated in at least one experimental session, and in most cases, more than one session such that overall data from 40 sessions was available for analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of patients and sessions in the Methods section.

claim: Patients correctly recalled both associated items on 75.43% (s.d.: 13.3) of the trials on average.
source: On average, patients correctly recalled both associated items on 75.43% (s.d.: 13.3) of the trials (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific behavioral performance data with mean and standard deviation, and references Figure 1B.

claim: The chance level for hits in this task is 16.6%.
source: Note that chance level in this task for hits and misses is 16.6 and 83.3%, respectively (indicated by dashed horizontal lines), and not 50% for both (see Methods for further details).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the chance level and provides a calculation in the Methods section.

claim: 232 putative single and multi-units were recorded, of which 218 were used for analysis.
source: Altogether 232 putative single and multi-units were recorded of which 218 were used for further analysis (14 units were rejected because of too low firing rates; see Methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of recorded units and those used for analysis.

claim: Units were classified into 82 putative single-units and 136 putative multi-units.
source: These units were classified into single-units and multi-units using an automatic procedure based on waveshape homogeneity and inter-spike intervals (ISIs; Tankus et al., 2009), resulting in 82 putative single-units and 136 putative multi-units (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the classification results and references the method used.

claim: Most electrodes (73%) were located in the hippocampus.
source: Most electrodes (73%) were located in the hippocampus, the rest was located in adjacent MTL regions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of electrodes in the hippocampus.

claim: Neural firing during encoding was not modulated by memory for the time window of interest (2–3 s).
source: Neural firing during encoding was not modulated by memory for the time window of interest (2–3 s).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: Hits showed a sustained increase in firing rate compared to misses at a later time window (>3 s).
source: However, hits showed a sustained increase in firing rate compared to misses at a later time window (>3 s; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: LFPs for hits and misses did not differ in terms of event-related potentials (ERPs) or inter-trial phase coherence.
source: LFPs for hits and misses also did not differ in terms of event-related potentials (ERPs) or inter-trial phase coherence (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Hits showed decreased low frequency but increased high-frequency power compared to misses.
source: However, expected differences between hits and misses were obtained in broad band power (Burke et al., 2015), with hits showing decreased low frequency but increased high-frequency power.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and cites a previous study showing similar results.

claim: 192 significantly coupled spike-LFP pairs were found in the high-frequency range (40–80 Hz), of which 53 were coupled to the local LFP and 139 coupled to distal LFPs.
source: During the time window of interest (2–3 s), 192 significantly (Rayleigh test; pcorr <0.05; FDR-correction) coupled spike-LFP pairs were found in the high-frequency range (40–80 Hz), of which 53 were coupled to the local LFP (4.87% of all possible combinations) and 139 coupled to distal LFPs (2.49% of all possible combinations, Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of significant spike-LFP pairs and references a figure.

claim: The number of locally coupled pairs was significantly higher than chance.
source: The number of locally coupled pairs was significantly higher than chance (Randomization test; p<0.0001), whereas the number of distally coupled pairs was not (p>0.35).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the statistical test results comparing observed pairs to chance.

claim: Local SFC showed a pronounced peak in the fast gamma range (~65 Hz), which was substantially stronger compared to distal couplings.
source: Local SFC showed a pronounced peak in the fast gamma range (~65 Hz), which was substantially stronger compared to distal couplings (T-test; pcorr <0.05; Figure 2B; FDR-correction).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: The peak frequency of local SFC varied as a function of memory formation such that hits showed stronger SFC at a higher frequency (~70 Hz) than misses (~62 Hz).
source: Importantly, the peak frequency of local SFC varied as a function of memory formation such that hits showed stronger SFC at a higher frequency (~70 Hz) than misses (~62 Hz; T-test; pcorr <0.05; FDR-correction; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: Hits were characterized by significantly faster gamma frequencies compared to misses (T-test; t36=1.96; p=0.029; Cohen's d=0.32).
source: The results confirmed that hits were characterized by significantly faster gamma frequencies compared to misses (T-test; t36=1.96; p=0.029; Cohen's d=0.32; Figure 2D - left).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with detailed statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: 103 locally coupled (9.46%) and 387 distally coupled (6.93%) spike-field pairs were identified in the low-frequency ranges (2–40 Hz).
source: We identified 103 locally coupled (9.46%) and 387 distally coupled (6.93%) spike-field pairs (Rayleigh-test; pcorr<0.05; FDR-corrected; Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of significant spike-LFP pairs in the low-frequency range and references a figure.

claim: For both local and distal couplings in the low-frequency range, the number of significant pairs exceeded chance level.
source: For both local and distal couplings, the number of significant pairs exceeded chance level (randomization test; both p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the statistical test results comparing observed pairs to chance.

claim: Local couplings showed a peak PPC at around 5 Hz (and another peak at 13 Hz), whereas distal couplings showed a peak at around 8–9 Hz.
source: Local couplings showed a peak PPC at around 5 Hz (and another peak at 13 Hz), whereas distal couplings showed a peak at around 8–9 Hz (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the peak frequencies for local and distal couplings and references a figure.

claim: Distally coupled spike-field pairs showed stronger coupling for hits compared to misses in the fast theta frequency range (8–10 Hz) and higher SFC for misses compared to hits in the slower theta frequency range (5 Hz).
source: In contrast, distally coupled spike-field pairs showed stronger coupling for hits compared to misses in the fast theta frequency range (8–10 Hz) and higher SFC for misses compared to hits in the slower theta frequency range (5 Hz; Figure 3C, T-test; pcorr<0.05; FDR-corrected).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: Hits exhibited a slightly faster peak in theta SFC compared to misses (T-test; t206=3.49; p=2.99*10–4; Cohen's d=0.24).
source: This was confirmed by a peak detection analysis showing that hits exhibited a slightly faster peak in theta SFC compared to misses (T-test; t206=3.49; p=2.99*10–4; Cohen's d=0.24; Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with detailed statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: Hits show significantly positive PSIs throughout the theta frequency range, peaking at ~8 Hz.
source: The results indicate above chance PSIs have for hits peaking in the fast theta band (7–8 Hz).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding about phase slope index.

claim: Hits show significantly higher PSIs compared to misses in the theta frequency range.
source: In addition, hits show significantly higher PSIs compared to misses (Figure 4), whereas PSIs for misses do not differ from zero.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: More than half of the electrodes (58%) showed both local gamma coupling and distal theta coupling.
source: More than half of the electrodes (58%) were available for this analysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of electrodes showing both types of coupling and references a figure.

claim: Hits showed stronger theta phase to gamma amplitude coupling compared to misses (Wilcoxon test; z=3.7; p=8.92*10–5, Cohen's d=0.39).
source: Hits showed stronger theta phase to gamma amplitude coupling compared to misses (Figure 5D; Wilcoxon test; z=3.7; p=8.92*10–5, Cohen's d=0.39).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with detailed statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: 32 pairs of putative up-stream and down-stream units were available for co-firing analysis, 24 of which showed above threshold co-firing.
source: Overall, 32 pairs were available for this analysis, 24 of which showed above threshold co-firing (see Figure 6—source data 1 for detailed information about each pair).

claim: Hits showed significant above chance co-firing at lags 20–40 ms, whereas co-incidences for misses peaked at 60 ms.
source: Compared to baseline, hits showed significant above chance co-firing at lags 20–40 ms, whereas co-incidences for misses peaked at 60 ms (T-test; pcorr<0.05; FDR-correction; Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: Hits showed stronger co-firing compared to misses at 20 ms.
source: In addition, hits showed stronger co-firing compared to misses at 20 ms (T-test; pcorr<0.05; FDR-correction; Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: Co-firing for hits peaked significantly earlier compared to misses (t21=−3.201; p=0.004292; Cohen's d=−0.68).
source: A peak detection analysis revealed that co-firing for hits peaked significantly earlier compared to misses (t21=−3.201; p=0.004292; Cohen's d=−0.68; Figure 6D).

claim: The memory related co-firing effect was observed only when selecting pairs of single-/multi-units that were both locally coupled to gamma and distally coupled to theta.
source: Intriguingly, this memory related co-firing effect was observed only when selecting pairs of single-/multi-units that were both locally coupled to gamma and distally coupled to theta.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this specific condition for observing the co-firing effect.

claim: Analyzing all possible pairs of distally coupled theta units showed no differences in peak co-incidences between hits and misses (t126=−0.78; p=0.432).
source: Analyzing all possible pairs of distally coupled theta units showed no differences in peak co-incidences between hits and misses (t126=−0.78; p=0.432).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with statistical test results.

claim: Theta and gamma oscillations in the medial temporal lobe are suggested to play a critical role for human memory formation via establishing synchrony in neural assemblies.
source: Theta and gamma oscillations in the medial temporal lobe are suggested to play a critical role for human memory formation via establishing synchrony in neural assemblies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background claim.

claim: Synchrony facilitates efficient information transfer between neurons and enhances synaptic plasticity, both of which benefit episodic memory formation.
source: Arguably, such synchrony facilitates efficient information transfer between neurons and enhances synaptic plasticity, both of which benefit episodic memory formation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a theoretical claim.

claim: Episodic memory relies on efficient information transmission within the medial temporal lobe.
source: Episodic memory relies on efficient information transmission within the medial temporal lobe (MTL; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Fell et al., 2001; Solomon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The strengthening of synaptic connections between neurons that are active during the experience of an episode depends critically on the temporal structure of neural firing.
source: The strengthening of synaptic connections between neurons that are active during the experience of an episode depends critically on the temporal structure of neural firing (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 2001; Hebb, 1949; Wespatat et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on synaptic plasticity.

claim: Brain oscillations at theta (~3–9 Hz) and gamma (~40–80 Hz) frequencies in the human MTL have been proposed to promote the formation of memories through the synchronization of neural firing in the MTL.
source: Accordingly, brain oscillations at theta (~3–9 Hz) and gamma (~40–80 Hz) frequencies in the human MTL have been proposed to promote the formation of memories through the synchronization of neural firing in the MTL (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Jutras and Buffalo, 2010; Huerta and Lisman, 1995; Hyman et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stronger phase-coupling of neural firing in theta oscillations has been observed during successful compared to unsuccessful encoding.
source: For instance, stronger phase-coupling of neural firing in theta (Rutishauser et al., 2010) oscillations has been observed during successful compared to unsuccessful encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A similar result has been obtained in macaques for the high gamma oscillations (>60 Hz).
source: A similar result has been obtained in macaques for the high gamma oscillations (>60 Hz; Jutras et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in macaques.

claim: Increased cross-frequency coupling (CFC) between theta-phase and the power of gamma oscillations for successfully encoded memory items has been reported in the human MTL.
source: Furthermore, increased cross-frequency coupling (CFC) between theta-phase and the power of gamma oscillations for successfully encoded memory items has also been reported in the human MTL (Griffiths et al., 2021; Lega et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Relatively faster oscillations integrate neural spikes over shorter time windows compared to relatively slower oscillations.
source: Relatively faster oscillations integrate neural spikes over shorter time windows compared to relatively slower oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle in the introduction.

claim: A neural assembly which synchronizes firing at faster oscillations is more likely to drive a down-stream neural assembly compared to synchronization at slower oscillations.
source: Therefore, a neural assembly which synchronizes firing at faster oscillations is more likely to drive a down-stream neural assembly compared to synchronization at slower oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical inference based on membrane potential dynamics.

claim: Fast (~65 Hz), but not slow (~40 Hz), gamma oscillations in rodents and humans have been demonstrated to reflect memory encoding processes.
source: This may be the reason for why fast (~65 Hz), but not slow (~40 Hz), gamma oscillations in rodents (Colgin et al., 2009) and humans Griffiths et al., 2019 have been demonstrated to reflect memory encoding processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in rodents and humans.

claim: A recent study demonstrated a role of sleep spindles for modulating short-latency co-firing between neurons in the lateral anterior temporal cortex.
source: A recent study demonstrated a role of sleep spindles for modulating short-latency co-firing between neurons in the lateral anterior temporal cortex (Dickey et al., 2021), which is consistent with the idea that oscillations in principle can regulate efficient information transfer between neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Enhanced local spike-LFP coupling for later successfully recognized pictures in the high gamma but not low gamma band has been observed in the hippocampal formation of macaques.
source: Enhanced local spike-LFP coupling for later successfully recognized pictures in the high gamma but not low gamma band has been observed in the hippocampal formation of macaques (Jutras et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in macaques.

claim: Other studies in rodents have identified different roles for fast vs slow gamma oscillations in the hippocampus, with fast gamma oscillations reflecting the routing of information into the hippocampus and slow gamma oscillations reflecting the routing of information out of the hippocampus.
source: Other studies in rodents have identified different roles for fast vs slow gamma oscillations in the hippocampus, with fast gamma oscillations reflecting the routing of information into the hippocampus and slow gamma oscillations reflecting the routing of information out of the hippocampus (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in rodents.

claim: Consistent results were obtained in humans showing that fast gamma oscillations positively predict encoding, whereas slow gamma oscillations positively predict retrieval of memories.
source: Consistent results were obtained in humans showing that fast gamma oscillations positively predict encoding, whereas slow gamma oscillations positively predict retrieval of memories (Griffiths et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in humans.

claim: Dissociations between slow and fast theta oscillations in humans have been reported previously.
source: Dissociations between slow and fast theta oscillations in humans have been reported previously (Lega et al., 2012; Goyal et al., 2020), albeit slow theta in these studies was considerably slower than reported here (i.e. ~2–4 Hz as opposed to 4–6 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The frequency of theta correlates positively with running speed in rodents and humans.
source: It is well documented that the frequency of theta correlates positively with running speed in rodents (Sławińska and Kasicki, 1998) and humans (Goyal et al., 2020), and that running speed-induced changes correlate with memory outcome (Richard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased inter-areal theta phase synchronization plays a crucial role for memory formation.
source: This result is in line with previous studies demonstrating a crucial role of inter-areal theta phase synchronization for memory formation (Solomon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased cross-frequency coupling between theta and gamma has been reported for memory encoding in the human MTL.
source: This result is in line with a previous study reporting similar results (Lega et al., 2016) and extends these findings to microwire recordings and links it with spike-LFP coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fast oscillations regulate local connectivity, slower oscillations regulate long-range connectivity, and CFC enables efficient interfacing between the local gamma and the long-range theta networks.
source: This result is consistent with current network models where fast oscillations regulate local connectivity, slower oscillations regulate long-range connectivity, and CFC enables efficient interfacing between the local gamma and the long-range theta networks (Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Roux and Uhlhaas, 2014; von Stein and Sarnthein, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The results are consistent with previous findings showing short-latency co-firing between neurons during memory processes.
source: These results are consistent with previous findings (Dickey et al., 2021) and support the idea that oscillations play a crucial role for memory formation because they enable efficient signal transmission and thereby affect synaptic plasticity (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Buzsáki, 2010; Jutras and Buffalo, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inter-regional phase synchronization can be a consequence rather than the cause of connectivity.
source: The idea that synchronized inter-regional oscillations reflect effective communication has recently been questioned by a study showing that inter-regional phase synchronization can be a consequence rather than the cause of connectivity (Schneider et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research questioning the causal role of oscillations.

claim: Successful encoding of memories depends not only on the input from surrounding MTL areas into the hippocampus but also on the output of the hippocampal system into those areas.
source: This result parallels other studies in humans showing that successful encoding of memories depends not only on the input from surrounding MTL areas into the hippocampus but also on the output of the hippocampal system into those areas, and indeed on the dynamic recurrent interaction between these input and output paths (Maass et al., 2014; Koster et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in humans.

claim: Studies in macaques showed that attention increases spike-LFP coupling while not affecting firing rates.
source: Studies in macaques showed that attention increases spike-LFP coupling while not affecting firing rates (Fries et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in macaques.
